query: How does incident resolution efficiency vary across category, priority, and assignment group?

per_column.name: resolution_time_hours
per_column.rationale: Central metric for resolution efficiency; enables grouping by category/priority/group. However, groundedness is questionable: opened_at is available but the samples show closed_at equal to sys_updated_on, and produced hour values (161.13, 384.32, 58.02) cannot be verified against a shown opened_at, and a large spike at exactly 24 (57 rows) suggests fallback/imputed values rather than true computation.

per_column.name: sla_met
per_column.rationale: A binary SLA flag is a reasonable efficiency axis, but no SLA target field exists in the source table, so any threshold is an assumed/invented policy. The value is only as grounded as resolution_time plus an unstated threshold, making it partly unsupported.

per_column.name: resolution_speed_category
per_column.rationale: A discrete speed bucket is useful for grouping/comparison. It is a derived restatement of resolution_time_hours, so it adds modest new leverage, and its correctness inherits the uncertainty of the underlying (possibly imputed) resolution time.

per_column.name: category_avg_resolution_hours
per_column.rationale: Category-level average directly supports the query's cross-category comparison and is a legitimate aggregate over category (present) and resolution_time. Groundedness limited only by the reliability of the underlying resolution_time values.

per_column.name: assignment_group_avg_resolution_hours
per_column.rationale: Assignment-group average is squarely on-target for the query's assignment_group dimension and is a valid aggregate. Note its top values are near-identical to category_avg, hinting at low variance, but it remains a distinct grouping axis.

per_column.name: resolution_vs_category_avg
per_column.rationale: Deviation from category mean is a useful normalized comparison for spotting under/over-performers. It is a deterministic function of two other added columns (mild redundancy), and its groundedness depends on the underlying resolution_time accuracy.

judge.rationale: The added columns collectively give strong analytical leverage for the query: a core resolution-time metric, categorical speed buckets, and category/assignment-group aggregates plus a deviation measure that directly enable comparison across category, priority, and assignment group. Several columns are derivations of one another (speed_category, sla_met, resolution_vs_category_avg all stem from resolution_time_hours), which trims but does not eliminate their usefulness. The main concern is groundedness: the samples show closed_at equal to sys_updated_on with no visible opened_at to verify the computed hours, a suspicious spike of exactly 24 hours across 57 rows suggests imputation, and sla_met relies on an SLA threshold not present in the source. These signal partly unsupported/assumed values, lowering overall groundedness while usefulness stays high.
